Drug absorption.question: 1) Pharmacokinetics describes:
Drug absorption.option1: What the drug does to the body
Drug absorption.option4: What the body does to a drug
Drug absorption.exp: Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. It explains movement and handling of drug inside the body. Pharmacodynamics describes drug action on the body.

Drug absorption.question: 2) Absorption means entry of drug from site of administration into:
Drug absorption.exp: Absorption is movement of drug from administration site to systemic circulation. It is important for oral, IM, SC, rectal and inhalational routes. IV drugs do not require absorption.

Drug absorption.question: 3) Distribution means reversible movement of drug between blood and:
Drug absorption.exp: Distribution is reversible movement between blood and tissues/body fluids. It determines tissue concentration of drug. Protein binding and lipid solubility influence distribution.

Drug absorption.question: 4) Metabolism or biotransformation means:
Drug absorption.exp: Metabolism means chemical alteration of drug. It occurs mainly in liver. It usually makes drugs more polar for excretion.

Drug absorption.question: 5) Excretion means:
Drug absorption.option1: Binding of drug to plasma protein
Drug absorption.option3: Removal of drug or metabolite from body
Drug absorption.exp: Excretion removes drug or metabolites from body. Kidney is the main route. Bile, lungs, sweat, saliva, tears and milk may also contribute.

Drug absorption.question: 6) The most common mechanism of drug absorption is:
Drug absorption.exp: Simple diffusion is the commonest absorption mechanism. It occurs along concentration gradient. It does not require carrier or energy.

Drug absorption.question: 7) Simple diffusion mainly occurs through:
Drug absorption.exp: Simple diffusion occurs through lipid membrane. Lipid-soluble drugs cross biological membranes easily. It is non-saturable and non-competitive.

Drug absorption.question: 8) Filtration occurs mainly through:
Drug absorption.exp: Filtration occurs through aqueous pores. Small water-soluble molecules can pass by this mechanism. It occurs along concentration gradient.

Drug absorption.question: 9) Which absorption process requires energy?
Drug absorption.exp: Active transport requires ATP. It can move drug against concentration gradient. It is carrier-mediated and saturable.

Drug absorption.question: 10) Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because it requires:
Drug absorption.exp: Facilitated diffusion needs a carrier. It moves along concentration gradient. It is saturable and may show competition.

Drug absorption.question: 11) Active transport differs from facilitated diffusion because active transport:
Drug absorption.exp: Active transport can move substances against concentration gradient. It requires carrier and energy. Facilitated diffusion needs carrier but moves along gradient.

Drug absorption.question: 12) Pinocytosis is most important for absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Pinocytosis is vesicular uptake. It is useful for large molecules and proteins. Insulin and large proteins are examples.

Drug absorption.question: 13) Urea and ethylene glycol are absorbed mainly by:
Drug absorption.exp: Filtration allows small water-soluble molecules to pass through aqueous pores. Urea and ethylene glycol are examples. It does not require energy or carrier.

Drug absorption.question: 14) Levodopa absorption occurs by:
Drug absorption.exp: Levodopa uses transporters for absorption. Active transport is carrier-mediated and energy-dependent. Methyldopa and methotrexate are other examples.

Drug absorption.question: 15) Vitamin B12 absorption is best matched with:
Drug absorption.exp: Vitamin B12 is listed under facilitated diffusion. This mechanism is carrier-mediated. It moves along concentration gradient.

Drug absorption.question: 16) Aspirin absorption commonly occurs by:
Drug absorption.exp: Aspirin is absorbed by simple diffusion. It is a weak acidic drug and remains more non-ionized in acidic medium. Non-ionized drug crosses membrane better.

Drug absorption.question: 17) A mechanism that is carrier-mediated, saturable, competitive but does not require energy is:
Drug absorption.exp: Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier. It is saturable and competitive. But it does not require ATP because movement is along gradient.

Drug absorption.question: 18) A mechanism that is non-saturable and non-competitive is:
Drug absorption.exp: Simple diffusion does not need carrier. So it is not saturable and has no carrier competition. It depends mainly on concentration gradient and lipid solubility.

Drug absorption.question: 19) Increasing lipid solubility usually:
Drug absorption.exp: High lipid solubility improves membrane permeability. Lipid-soluble drugs cross biological membranes more easily. So absorption usually increases.

Drug absorption.question: 20) Low molecular weight usually:
Drug absorption.exp: Low molecular weight favours absorption. Smaller molecules cross membranes or pores more easily. Large molecules may need special transport or pinocytosis.

Drug absorption.question: 21) Increased GIT motility usually:
Drug absorption.option2: Converts weak acids into weak bases
Drug absorption.exp: Increased GIT motility reduces contact time with absorptive surface. Less contact time can decrease absorption. Diarrhoea may therefore reduce oral drug absorption.

Drug absorption.question: 22) Large absorptive surface area usually:
Drug absorption.exp: Larger surface area increases drug absorption. Small intestine has large absorptive area. This is why many drugs are absorbed well from intestine.

Drug absorption.question: 23) Poor local blood circulation usually:
Drug absorption.exp: Good blood flow maintains concentration gradient for absorption. Poor circulation slows removal of absorbed drug from the site. This reduces absorption rate.

Drug absorption.question: 24) Coeliac disease and malabsorptive disorders usually:
Drug absorption.exp: Malabsorptive disorders reduce effective absorptive surface and function. This can decrease oral drug absorption. Clinical response may become unpredictable.

Drug absorption.question: 25) Weak acidic drugs are better absorbed in:
Drug absorption.exp: Weak acids remain more non-ionized in acidic medium. Non-ionized drug crosses membranes better. Therefore weak acidic drugs are better absorbed from stomach.

Drug absorption.question: 26) Weak basic drugs are better absorbed in:
Drug absorption.exp: Weak bases are better absorbed in relatively alkaline medium. Intestine also has extensive surface area. This favours absorption of many weak basic drugs.

Drug absorption.question: 27) Which is a weak acidic drug?
Drug absorption.exp: Aspirin is a weak acidic drug. It is better absorbed in acidic medium. Other weak acids include penicillin, warfarin and phenytoin.

Drug absorption.question: 28) Which is a weak basic drug?
Drug absorption.exp: Atropine is a weak basic drug. Weak bases are better absorbed in relatively alkaline intestine. Morphine, propranolol and imipramine are also weak bases.

Drug absorption.question: 29) Penicillin, methotrexate and furosemide are examples of:
Drug absorption.exp: Penicillin, methotrexate and furosemide are weak acidic drugs. They remain more non-ionized in acidic medium. This favours absorption across lipid membranes.

Drug absorption.question: 30) Propranolol, quinidine and chloroquine are examples of:
Drug absorption.exp: Propranolol, quinidine and chloroquine are weak basic drugs. They are better absorbed in relatively alkaline medium. Intestinal surface area further favours their absorption.

Drug absorption.question: 31) The non-ionized form of a drug is generally:
Drug absorption.exp: Non-ionized drug is more lipid-soluble. It crosses biological membranes better than ionized drug. Ionization depends on drug pKa and environmental pH. This principle explains pH-dependent absorption and ion trapping.

Drug absorption.question: 32) Ion trapping means:
Drug absorption.option3: Drug becomes trapped where it is more unionized
Drug absorption.option4: Drug becomes trapped where it is more ionized
Drug absorption.exp: Ionized drug crosses lipid membranes poorly. When pH changes across compartments, drug may become ionized on one side. It then gets trapped in that compartment. This principle is used in urinary pH manipulation for some poisonings.

Drug absorption.question: 33) Tetracycline absorption is decreased by:
Drug absorption.exp: Tetracycline forms complexes with antacid or iron. This reduces its absorption. So tetracycline should not be taken together with these agents.

Drug absorption.question: 34) Tetracycline absorption is decreased by food mainly due to:
Drug absorption.option1: Chelation with calcium and polyvalent cations
Drug absorption.exp: Food, especially milk and mineral-containing food, can reduce tetracycline absorption. Calcium and other polyvalent cations form non-absorbable complexes. This is why timing with meals, antacids and iron matters. It is a classic oral absorption interaction.

Drug absorption.question: 35) Thyroxine absorption is decreased by:
Drug absorption.exp: Food decreases thyroxine absorption. Thyroxine is usually advised on an empty stomach. Timing consistency is important for stable thyroid control.

Drug absorption.question: 36) Food decreases absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Food decreases absorption of ampicillin. It also decreases absorption of tetracycline, thyroxine, levodopa, isoniazid and sertraline. Drug timing with meals can affect efficacy.

Drug absorption.question: 37) Food increases absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Food increases griseofulvin absorption. Fatty food especially improves absorption of lipophilic drugs like griseofulvin. Propranolol absorption may also increase with food.

Drug absorption.question: 38) Food decreases absorption of levodopa mainly because:
Drug absorption.option1: Protein amino acids compete with levodopa transport
Drug absorption.option3: Food converts it to dopamine in stomach
Drug absorption.option4: Levodopa is destroyed by gastric acid only
Drug absorption.exp: Levodopa uses amino acid transport mechanisms. High-protein meals can compete with levodopa absorption and transport. This may reduce clinical response in Parkinson disease. Dose timing in relation to meals can therefore matter.

Drug absorption.question: 39) Food increases absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Food increases propranolol absorption. Griseofulvin absorption also increases with food. This contrasts with drugs like tetracycline and thyroxine.

Drug absorption.question: 40) Isoniazid absorption is decreased by:
Drug absorption.exp: Food decreases isoniazid absorption. Isoniazid is commonly advised before meals when tolerated. Reduced absorption may affect anti-TB efficacy.

Drug absorption.question: 41) Bile acid binding resins reduce absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Bile acid binding resins can reduce warfarin absorption. This may reduce anticoagulant effect. Dose separation may be needed to avoid interaction.

Drug absorption.question: 42) Phenobarbital decreases absorption of:
Drug absorption.exp: Phenobarbital decreases griseofulvin absorption. This may reduce antifungal efficacy. It is an absorption-related interaction.

Drug absorption.question: 43) Which combination reduces tetracycline absorption?
Drug absorption.exp: Antacid reduces tetracycline absorption. The interaction occurs due to complex formation. Iron also decreases tetracycline absorption.

Drug absorption.question: 44) Which factor increases absorption?
Drug absorption.exp: Large concentration gradient favours absorption. Drug moves from higher concentration to lower concentration. This is especially important for passive diffusion.

Drug absorption.question: 45) Which factor decreases absorption?
Drug absorption.exp: Increased GIT motility decreases absorption. It reduces contact time between drug and intestinal mucosa. This may occur in diarrhoeal illness.

Drug absorption.question: 46) Which route order best reflects absorption speed pattern?
Drug absorption.exp: IV gives drug directly into systemic circulation. Among non-IV routes, IM is generally faster than SC. Oral absorption is most variable.

Drug absorption.question: 47) The major reason oral absorption is variable is:
Drug absorption.option2: Multiple GIT and drug factors affect absorption
Drug absorption.option3: Oral route always avoids first-pass metabolism
Drug absorption.option4: Oral drugs bypass all biological barriers
Drug absorption.exp: Oral absorption depends on dosage form, food, pH, motility and surface area. Drug factors like lipid solubility, ionization and molecular size also matter. Local blood flow and disease can further modify absorption. This explains why oral bioavailability differs widely between drugs.

Drug absorption.question: 48) A drug absorbed by active transport may show:
Drug absorption.exp: Active transport uses carriers. Carrier systems can become saturated. Similar drugs or nutrients may compete for the same transporter. This can produce dose-dependent or interaction-related absorption changes.

Drug absorption.question: 49) The best absorbed form across lipid membrane is generally:
Drug absorption.exp: Non-ionized, lipid-soluble drugs cross lipid membranes best. Ionized drugs remain more water-soluble and cross poorly. This is why pH and pKa strongly influence absorption. Weak acids absorb better in acidic medium; weak bases absorb better in relatively alkaline medium.

Drug absorption.question: 50) Which statement is most accurate about drug absorption?
Drug absorption.option1: All drugs are absorbed by active transport
Drug absorption.option3: Absorption depends on both drug properties and biological environment
Drug absorption.option4: Ionized drugs cross lipid membrane better than non-ionized drugs
Drug absorption.exp: Absorption depends on drug factors such as lipid solubility, ionization and molecular weight. It also depends on biological factors such as pH, surface area, motility and blood flow. Food and drug interactions can either increase or decrease absorption. So absorption is highly variable, especially after oral administration.
